suites.name: Material Requirements and Functional Design
suites.resp: Target properties, functionality, specifications and engineering constraints

hybrid: Non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II and III

ibc.ic: The software should accept an initial candidate material composition, baseline physical properties, preliminary material dimensions, intended functionality, reference operating state, baseline geometry, existing manufacturing capabilities, preliminary design targets and initial optimisation variables. Where optimisation is performed, the starting design may contain an initial material configuration, initial unit-cell topology, proposed dimensional parameters, an initial performance estimate and a reference manufacturing cost.
ibc.bc: The software should accept prescribed limits on operating temperatures, pressures, mechanical loads, electrical fields, electromagnetic frequencies, material density, dimensions, mass, performance, energy consumption, production cost, toxicity, environmental exposure and manufacturing tolerances. These are principally design constraints rather than PDE boundary conditions. If physical simulations are included, their actual boundary conditions must be defined in the relevant physics suite.

suites.num: Objective weights, variable bounds, constraint tolerances, candidate population and stopping criteria

cvv.cal: Material selection weights, empirical design-performance correlations and decision-model parameters should be calibrated using historical material performance data, engineering design records and application-specific testing.
cvv.ver: The software should test requirement evaluation, constraint satisfaction, dimensional consistency, optimisation convergence, ranking reproducibility and correct identification of infeasible designs.
cvv.val: Recommended materials should be compared with independently tested alternatives for the same engineering application. Validation should determine whether candidates satisfy actual mechanical, thermal, electrical, optical, chemical, economic or other stated requirements.
cvv.exp: Verified optimisation behaviour, design compliance reports, candidate ranking accuracy, prediction errors and documented design limitations.

suites.name: Chemical Composition and Material Selection
suites.resp: Elements, compounds, dopants, constituent selection and property databases

ibc.ic: Initial elemental compositions, atomic fractions, mole fractions, mass fractions, precursor purity, dopant concentrations, initial chemical phases, initial oxidation states, impurity concentrations, initial temperature, initial pressure, reference chemical potential and initial phase fractions should be accepted. For compositional evolution simulations, the software should also accept initial local composition fields, segregation profiles and initial concentration gradients.
ibc.bc: Closed-system elemental conservation, prescribed chemical reservoirs, fixed chemical potentials, imposed species concentrations, external precursor supply, species inflow and outflow, impermeable boundaries, prescribed chemical fluxes, chemical exchange with surrounding media and equilibrium exchange with adjacent phases should be supported. For equilibrium phase calculations, many of these are thermodynamic constraints rather than spatial boundary conditions.

suites.num: Thermodynamic minimisation tolerance, composition grid, phase search and property interpolation

cvv.cal: Composition-dependent property relations, phase stability parameters, thermodynamic database interactions and mixture models should be calibrated using experimentally characterised materials.
cvv.ver: The software should test elemental balance, phase fraction consistency, constrained composition calculations, limiting mixture cases and numerical convergence of thermodynamic models.
cvv.val: Predicted phase fractions, solubility limits, phase transitions and material properties should be compared with independent composition measurements, phase diagrams, calorimetry, diffraction and property tests.
cvv.exp: Phase prediction accuracy, property errors, composition sensitivity, thermodynamic parameter uncertainty and validated composition ranges.

suites.name: Atomic, Molecular and Crystal Structure
suites.resp: Atomic geometry, molecular structure, crystallography and crystal defects

ibc.ic: Initial Cartesian or fractional atomic coordinates, atomic identities, molecular bond configurations, crystal lattice vectors, unit-cell dimensions, atomic velocities, atomic charges, spin configurations, initial crystal orientation, vacancy and interstitial locations, dislocation configurations, surface terminations, adsorbed molecules, initial atomic temperature and pressure, and initial molecular conformations should be provided where required by the selected model.
ibc.bc: Periodic boundaries in one, two or three directions, free surfaces, vacuum-separated slabs, fixed atoms, constrained atomic displacements, externally applied forces, prescribed strains, applied pressure, imposed electric fields, magnetic fields and surface interactions should be supported. Molecular dynamics models should also permit suitable thermostat and barostat ensembles, reflecting boundaries where physically appropriate, and boundary treatment for finite molecular clusters.
ibc.note: Quantum calculations may require wavefunction boundary conditions, periodic Bloch conditions, electrostatic potential references and carefully specified charged-system treatments.

suites.num: Basis cutoff, k-point sampling, electronic convergence, structural relaxation and symmetry tolerances

cvv.cal: Where adjustable parameters exist, interatomic potentials, empirical electronic corrections and force-field parameters should be fitted to appropriate quantum reference calculations or experimental data. First-principles methods generally require convergence and approximation assessment rather than empirical calibration of every calculation.
cvv.ver: The software should test electronic convergence, basis-set and energy-cutoff convergence, k-point convergence, force consistency, stress consistency, symmetry preservation and structural optimisation stability.
cvv.val: Equilibrium lattice constants, crystal structures, elastic constants, phonon frequencies, defect energies, surface properties and other predictions should be compared with suitable experimental measurements or high-quality independent reference calculations, with the type of evidence clearly identified.
cvv.exp: Convergence records, crystal-structure differences, energy and force errors, property prediction errors and limits of transferability.

suites.name: Nanomaterial Geometry and Morphology
suites.resp: Nanoparticles, nanorods, fibres, tubes, sheets, films, pores and coatings

ibc.ic: Initial particle diameter, length, thickness, aspect ratio, spatial position, orientation, particle number density, size distribution, pore structure, surface roughness, initial agglomeration state, initial nanoparticle clusters, initial coating thickness, initial void fraction, core–shell geometry, seed positions and initial microstructural topology should be specified. For evolving geometries, the software should accept an initial surface mesh, level-set field, signed-distance field, voxel structure or parameterised geometry.
ibc.bc: Fixed external geometric constraints, prescribed particle containment, periodic representative-volume boundaries, particle–substrate contact, wall exclusion conditions, particle injection or removal boundaries, geometric symmetry, moving interfaces, deposition surfaces, prescribed surface growth rates and permitted domain expansion should be supported. Surface continuity, contact and nonpenetration conditions are important where particles or nanostructures interact mechanically.

suites.num: Geometry resolution, voxel size, particle sampling, surface reconstruction and mesh quality

cvv.cal: Image segmentation, particle detection, morphology reconstruction, statistical particle generation and surface reconstruction parameters should be calibrated against reference measurements and characterised samples.
cvv.ver: The software should test geometric volume, surface area, dimensional accuracy, particle counts, orientation calculations, pore connectivity, topology preservation and mesh conversion.
cvv.val: Reconstructed nanoparticles, nanorods, nanotubes, nanosheets, fibres, pores and coatings should be compared with independent SEM, TEM, AFM, tomography and profilometry measurements.
cvv.exp: Dimensional reconstruction errors, particle-size distribution agreement, surface and volume deviations, morphology classification accuracy and reconstruction uncertainty.

ibc.ic: Initial unit-cell geometry, lattice vectors, unit-cell periodicity, constituent material distributions, beam and strut thicknesses, resonator positions, resonator masses, effective initial stiffness estimates, initial mechanical deformation, initial prestress, initial actuator state, initial resonator displacement, initial electromagnetic or acoustic field states for transient analyses, and initial programmed configuration should be accepted.
ibc.bc: Periodic structural boundaries, Bloch–Floquet periodicity, prescribed displacement, fixed supports, applied forces and tractions, imposed macroscopic strain, imposed stress, electromagnetic periodic boundaries, acoustic radiation boundaries, absorbing boundaries, symmetry planes and finite-array edge boundaries should be supported. For resonant unit cells, the software must allow wave propagation phase relationships across opposite faces. For finite metamaterial structures, actual supports and edge conditions must replace idealised infinite periodicity where appropriate.

suites.num: Unit-cell discretisation, periodic mapping, Bloch sampling, eigenmode count and topology optimisation

cvv.cal: Unit-cell constitutive properties, resonator damping, contact behaviour, geometric imperfection distributions and effective-property models should be calibrated using physical unit-cell or array measurements.
cvv.ver: The software should test periodic boundary conditions, Bloch phase relations, eigenfrequency convergence, mesh independence, homogenisation consistency and effective-property extraction.
cvv.val: Fabricated unit cells and arrays should be tested for effective stiffness, Poisson's ratio, resonance frequency, dispersion, wave transmission, optical or electromagnetic response, acoustic attenuation and architectural stability.
cvv.exp: Effective-property prediction error, resonance-frequency error, bandgap-edge error, geometry sensitivity, finite-array differences and manufacturing defect sensitivity.

suites.name: Thermodynamics, Chemical Equilibrium and Phase Behaviour
suites.resp: Chemical potential, solubility, stability and phase transformation

formulations: Second and third laws of thermodynamics

ibc.ic: Initial chemical composition, temperature, pressure, phase fractions, dissolved gas concentrations, species activities, ionic strength, pH, precursor concentration, initial supersaturation, chemical potential estimates and initial metastable phases should be provided where relevant. For nonequilibrium phase evolution, initial local phase distributions and composition fields are also required.
ibc.bc: Prescribed temperature, pressure, volume, entropy or enthalpy constraints depending on the chosen thermodynamic ensemble; fixed elemental inventories; imposed chemical potentials; contact with chemical reservoirs; imposed external gas partial pressures; phase interface equilibrium conditions; and open-system material exchange should be supported. Pure equilibrium calculations do not necessarily involve physical spatial boundaries. When coupled to a transport solver, the chemical boundary conditions must be defined on the corresponding spatial domain.

suites.num: Phase equilibrium solver tolerance, composition discretisation, nonlinear equilibrium iterations

cvv.cal: Activity coefficient parameters, interaction coefficients, thermodynamic databases and nonideal solution models should be calibrated against phase equilibrium, solubility and calorimetric measurements.
cvv.ver: The software should test conservation of chemical elements, equilibrium convergence, phase stability conditions, limiting ideal solutions and consistency of thermodynamic derivatives.
cvv.val: Predicted phase diagrams, equilibrium compositions, solubilities, precipitation thresholds and transformation temperatures should be compared with independent experimental measurements.
cvv.exp: Phase equilibrium deviations, solubility prediction errors, transformation-temperature errors and thermodynamic uncertainty.

suites.resp: Reaction kinetics, nucleation, crystal growth and particle population evolution

ibc.ic: Initial precursor and intermediate species concentrations, product concentration, temperature, pressure, solvent composition, pH, supersaturation, initial seed particle sizes, nucleation site density, seed distribution, existing particle-size distribution, crystal phase, substrate properties, surface coverage, initial growth-front locations and initial reaction progress should be provided.

ibc.note: The model should also distinguish between reactions taking place throughout the fluid volume and reactions restricted to solid surfaces or interfaces.

suites.num: Reaction tolerance, time step, particle-size bins, stochastic nucleation sampling and interface tracking

cvv.cal: Reaction rate constants, activation energies, nucleation parameters, crystal growth rates, surface attachment coefficients, aggregation kernels and ripening parameters should be fitted against kinetic and morphological data.
cvv.ver: The software should test reaction mass balance, species conservation, population balance conservation, positivity, time-step independence, growth-front resolution and stochastic ensemble convergence.
cvv.val: Predicted reactant conversion, induction time, nucleation rates, nanorod dimensions, particle-size distributions, crystal orientation and morphology should be compared with independent growth experiments.
cvv.exp: Growth-rate prediction errors, nucleation-time errors, particle-size distribution agreement, morphology deviations, parameter identifiability and predictive operating ranges.

suites.resp: Surface chemistry, adhesion, adsorption, wetting and particle interactions

formulations: Interfacial mass and heat flux relations

ibc.bc: Prescribed surface charge or surface potential, surface chemical reaction flux, adsorption and desorption kinetics, liquid–solid wetting conditions, contact-angle constraints, capillary pressure conditions, particle adhesion and detachment, no-slip or slip fluid boundaries, thermal contact resistance, electrical interface resistance, membrane permeability and selective ion transport should be supported. At particle–particle and particle–substrate contacts, the software should accommodate suitable force, adhesion, steric and electrostatic interaction models.

suites.num: Surface resolution, electrostatic solver tolerance, adsorption integration and particle interaction cutoff

cvv.cal: Surface energies, adsorption constants, electrostatic interaction parameters, interfacial adhesion, contact-angle models and aggregation rates should be calibrated using surface and colloidal measurements.
cvv.ver: The software should test interfacial mass and charge conservation, numerical convergence of surface models, contact treatment, particle interaction limits and surface flux consistency.
cvv.val: Predictions should be compared with contact-angle measurements, zeta potential, adsorption isotherms, colloidal stability tests, adhesion tests and measured aggregation kinetics.
cvv.exp: Contact-angle errors, surface coverage prediction accuracy, colloidal stability classification performance and interfacial transport uncertainty.

suites.name: Fluid Dynamics and Porous-Media Transport
suites.resp: Flow, pressure, permeability, mixing and fluid–particle behaviour

ibc.ic: Initial velocity fields, pressure distributions, temperature fields, fluid densities, viscosities, species concentrations, particle distributions, gas and liquid volume fractions, porous-medium saturation, porosity, permeability, dissolved gas content, turbulence quantities and initial reactor filling levels should be available.
ibc.bc: Prescribed inlet velocity, mass flow rate, volumetric flow rate, inlet pressure, outlet pressure, traction or open boundaries, no-slip walls, partial-slip walls, moving walls, symmetry planes, periodic flow boundaries, permeable and impermeable surfaces, porous interfaces, specified fluid injection and withdrawal, multiphase inlet composition, wall roughness, capillary pressure and fluid–structure interface coupling should be supported.
ibc.note: For microscale fluid motion, appropriate slip, electroosmotic, capillary or rarefaction-related boundary treatments may be necessary. For porous media, the software should distinguish Darcy-scale boundaries from pore-resolved fluid boundaries.

suites.num: Mesh, CFL limit, pressure–velocity coupling, transport discretisation and porous-media solver tolerance

cvv.cal: Porous-medium permeability, hydraulic resistance, non-Newtonian rheological parameters, drag coefficients and closure models should be calibrated against measured pressure drop, flow and transport data.
cvv.ver: The software should test conservation, benchmark laminar flows, porous-media analytical solutions, mesh refinement, time-step convergence, turbulence-model implementation and interface coupling.
cvv.val: Predicted pressure drops, velocity profiles, residence-time distributions, pore-scale flow patterns, permeability, mixing, particle deposition and multiphase behaviour should be compared with flow-loop, reactor or microfluidic measurements.
cvv.exp: Pressure and flow errors, permeability prediction differences, mixing agreement, transport uncertainty and model limitations.

suites.resp: Temperature fields, thermal conduction, heating, cooling and thermal stability

ibc.ic: Initial temperature field, initial wall and substrate temperatures, initial heater temperature, initial thermal energy, initial material phase fractions, initial reaction heat state, initial electric current distribution where relevant, initial thermal stress state and initial temperatures of adjacent fluids should be specified.
ibc.bc: Prescribed temperature, prescribed heat flux, adiabatic insulation, convective heat transfer to fluids, radiative heat exchange, thermal contact resistance, imposed heater power, laser or microwave heat input, coupled solid–fluid heat transfer, phase-change interfaces, moving thermal boundaries, prescribed ambient temperature, heat-sink boundaries, periodic thermal conditions and symmetry conditions should be supported.
ibc.note: Nanoscale heat-transfer models may additionally require phonon scattering, interfacial energy transmission or ballistic transport boundary descriptions where the continuum Fourier approximation becomes inadequate.

suites.num: Thermal mesh, time integration, radiation resolution and thermal coupling tolerance

cvv.cal: Thermal conductivity, heat capacity, interface resistance, heat-transfer coefficients, emissivity and nanoscale transport coefficients should be calibrated against thermal measurements.
cvv.ver: The software should test standard conduction solutions, transient thermal benchmarks, energy conservation, interface heat-flux continuity, radiation solver accuracy and mesh/time-step convergence.
cvv.val: Temperature profiles, thermal diffusivity, heat flux, heating and cooldown times, hotspots and interfacial thermal behaviour should be compared with thermal camera data, thermocouples, calorimetry, thermoreflectance and other appropriate measurements.
cvv.exp: Temperature errors, heat-flow errors, thermal time-constant deviations, interfacial resistance uncertainty and thermal model validity ranges.

cvv.ver: The software should test charge conservation, Poisson solver accuracy, carrier transport benchmark cases, electrochemical flux consistency, current balance and mesh/time-step convergence.

ibc.note: For frequency-domain calculations, an initial physical field state is generally unnecessary; excitation frequency, source amplitude and appropriate boundary conditions are required instead. For optical metasurfaces, the software should support both unit-cell periodic analysis and finite-aperture simulation, including incidence angle and polarisation dependence.
ibc.bc: Perfect electric conductor boundaries, perfect magnetic conductor boundaries, impedance boundaries, absorbing boundaries, perfectly matched layers, scattering and radiation boundaries, prescribed electric or magnetic fields, incident plane-wave conditions, waveguide port conditions, periodic electromagnetic boundaries, Bloch–Floquet phase-shift conditions, symmetry boundaries, dielectric interface continuity, conductive sheet conditions, optical input/output ports and electromagnetic coupling to external circuits should be supported.

suites.num: Frequency sampling, wavelength resolution, mesh order, absorbing layers, eigenmodes and Bloch conditions

cvv.cal: Frequency-dependent optical constants, dielectric dispersion, conductive losses, surface roughness, resonator damping and effective constitutive parameters should be calibrated against measured electromagnetic spectra.
cvv.ver: The software should test analytical scattering solutions, cavity resonances, waveguide modes, Maxwell boundary consistency, absorbing boundary performance, Bloch periodicity, energy balance and frequency/mesh convergence.
cvv.val: Simulated reflection, transmission, absorption, resonance frequencies, beam steering, optical phase, polarisation conversion, photonic bandgaps and field patterns should be compared with independent spectroscopy, microwave, terahertz, optical and near-field measurements.
cvv.exp: Resonance shifts, spectral errors, bandgap deviations, phase errors, optical efficiency differences and effective-property retrieval uncertainty.

numGroups.title: Simulation type and mathematical problem configuration
numGroups.part: UNIVERSAL NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: The software should allow engineers to specify whether the analysis is steady-state, stationary equilibrium, transient, time-dependent, frequency-domain, eigenvalue, modal, nonlinear static, dynamic, quasistatic, harmonic, stochastic, probabilistic, parameter-sweep, optimisation, inverse or coupled multiphysics.

It should provide options for deterministic and stochastic solutions; linear and nonlinear problems; explicit and implicit mathematical formulations; strongly and weakly coupled physics; forward and inverse calculations; local and global optimisation; and single-scale or multiscale modelling.

The configuration should also specify whether the computational problem is one-dimensional, two-dimensional, axisymmetric, two-and-a-half-dimensional, three-dimensional or based on an atomistic, molecular, periodic-cell, network, graph or reduced-order representation.

Other settings include the selected physics, active dependent variables, degrees of freedom, chosen governing models, constitutive formulations, source terms, reference configuration, solution continuation strategy and numerical assumptions.

numGroups.title: Computational domain and geometry discretisation
numGroups.part: UNIVERSAL NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: The software should accept the computational domain dimensions, geometry dimensionality, coordinate system, origin, coordinate orientation, unit scale, geometric tolerance and characteristic length.
It should support Cartesian, cylindrical, spherical, curvilinear, lattice-based and material-coordinate representations as appropriate.
The parameters should include the number of subdomains, material regions, surfaces, geometric boundaries, embedded inclusions, pores, particles, resonators, crystal grains and periodic unit cells.

For large metamaterial structures, the numerical configuration should include the number of repeated unit cells, supercell dimensions, representative-volume size, geometric grading, periodicity and finite-array extent.
For nanomaterials, it should support atomic or particle counts, simulation box dimensions, particle spatial distribution, seed density, initial surface discretisation and microstructure resolution.
The software should also permit geometric defeaturing tolerances, topology-preservation settings, surface healing tolerances, mesh-to-geometry projection tolerances and geometry scaling parameters.

numGroups.title: Spatial mesh generation and resolution
numGroups.part: UNIVERSAL NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: Typical parameters should include the selected mesh topology, element type, mesh generation algorithm, global element size, minimum element size, maximum element size, local mesh size, mesh growth rate and grading factor.
The engineer should be able to specify the number of nodes, elements, cells and degrees of freedom, as well as structured versus unstructured meshing.

Supported element families should include triangular, quadrilateral, tetrahedral, hexahedral, prism, pyramid, beam, shell, plate, cohesive, interface, surface, voxel and polyhedral elements where compatible with the numerical method.

Mesh controls should include element aspect ratio, skewness, orthogonality, warpage, Jacobian quality, minimum angle, maximum angle, curvature resolution, proximity resolution, small-feature preservation and boundary representation accuracy.

For nanostructures, local refinement should be available at grain boundaries, interfaces, nanorod tips, nanoparticle surfaces, cracks, defects, pores, chemical reaction fronts, growing crystals and high-field regions.

For metamaterials, additional mesh controls should govern thin struts, lattice junctions, resonator gaps, split-ring openings, electromagnetic hotspots, acoustic cavities, periodic surfaces and sharply varying effective material properties.

numGroups.title: Mesh refinement, adaptation and convergence
numGroups.part: UNIVERSAL NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: The software should support uniform mesh refinement, local adaptive refinement, anisotropic refinement, hierarchical refinement, adaptive coarsening, remeshing and moving-mesh methods.

Typical settings include refinement levels, maximum refinement depth, refinement thresholds, coarsening thresholds, target element counts, maximum degrees of freedom, error-indicator selection and adaptation frequency.

Adaptive refinement criteria may be based on temperature gradients, concentration gradients, velocity gradients, stress concentrations, electromagnetic field gradients, acoustic pressure gradients, phase-field interfaces, nucleation regions, moving growth fronts or estimated discretisation error.

For evolving nanomaterials, the software should provide controls for mesh deformation, moving-interface tracking, mesh regeneration, interpolation of old solution fields onto new meshes and conservation during remapping.
For metamaterial analysis, it should preserve periodic mesh correspondence, unit-cell boundary mappings, symmetry constraints and wave-phase relationships during refinement.
Mesh-convergence controls should include refinement sequences, extrapolation strategy, target solution changes, estimated error thresholds and convergence stopping criteria.

numGroups.title: Finite-element numerical discretisation
numGroups.part: UNIVERSAL NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: For finite-element simulations, the numerical parameters should include element interpolation order, polynomial degree, basis function family, continuity class, mixed-element formulation, reduced or full integration, numerical quadrature order and stabilisation method.
The software should support suitable continuous Galerkin, discontinuous Galerkin, mixed finite-element, enriched finite-element and extended finite-element formulations.

Numerical controls should include the selected primary variables, interpolation compatibility, pressure–velocity stability, displacement–pressure stability, locking prevention, hourglass control, contact element settings, cohesive element discretisation and large-deformation treatment.
For coupled multiphysics, engineers should be able to select whether different physical fields use the same mesh or separate meshes, as well as field interpolation and intermesh transfer strategies.

numGroups.title: Finite-volume and finite-difference discretisation
numGroups.part: UNIVERSAL NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: For finite-volume simulations, the software should support the selected control-volume arrangement, cell-centred or vertex-centred variable storage, face interpolation method, flux reconstruction method, gradient reconstruction and diffusion discretisation.

Numerical controls should include first-order or higher-order spatial accuracy, central differencing, upwind differencing, bounded high-resolution schemes, total variation diminishing schemes and appropriate flux-limiters.

For finite-difference simulations, users should be able to specify grid spacing, stencil width, approximation order, centred or one-sided differencing, compact finite-difference methods and treatment of irregular boundaries.
Advection stabilisation, positivity preservation, monotonicity, conservative flux handling and boundary extrapolation should be configurable.
For coupled reaction–transport calculations, the discretisation should prevent physically impossible negative concentrations where the chosen model requires nonnegative species quantities.

numGroups.title: Time integration and transient simulation
numGroups.part: UNIVERSAL NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: Typical parameters should include simulation start time, end time, total duration, initial time step, minimum time step, maximum time step and total permitted time steps.

The platform should support fixed and adaptive time stepping, implicit and explicit integration, first-order and higher-order schemes, backward Euler, Crank–Nicolson, Runge–Kutta, backward differentiation formulas, predictor–corrector methods and suitable symplectic integration for dynamical systems.

Time-step adaptation parameters should include absolute and relative local error tolerances, maximum permitted time-step growth, time-step reduction factors, rejection limits, safety factors and event-detection tolerances.
For transient chemical and thermal processes, time-step controls should resolve rapid reaction onset, nucleation bursts, phase transitions, thermal transients and moving growth fronts.
For transient metamaterials, time-step controls should resolve wave periods, resonator dynamics, switching events, actuator movement and nonlinear instabilities.
For atomistic simulations, time-step size should be chosen to resolve relevant atomic vibrations and fast dynamical processes rather than using continuum-scale time steps.

numGroups.title: Numerical stability and conservation parameters
numGroups.part: UNIVERSAL NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: The software should provide stability controls appropriate to the selected numerical schemes, including Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy limits, diffusive stability limits, reaction stiffness measures and wave propagation resolution criteria.

Other settings should include numerical damping, artificial viscosity where justified, slope limiting, flux limiting, positivity preservation, boundedness enforcement and appropriate stabilisation coefficients.
Conservation monitoring should cover mass, chemical elements, charge, momentum, energy and particle number or population moments where the mathematical formulation requires them.

Engineers should be able to set acceptable conservation residuals, allowable imbalance, maximum numerical overshoot and undershoot, and thresholds for terminating simulations when physical constraints are violated.

Stability controls should be matched to the mathematical model and numerical scheme. For example, explicit wave simulations and implicit stiff chemical reaction systems have substantially different numerical requirements.

numGroups.title: Linear algebra and linear solver parameters
numGroups.part: UNIVERSAL NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: Typical settings should include direct or iterative linear solution, sparse matrix storage, matrix assembly method, matrix-free operation, numerical precision and linear system scaling.
Direct solver settings should include matrix factorisation method, pivoting strategy, reordering algorithm, fill-in controls and numerical stability thresholds.
Iterative solver options may include conjugate gradient, GMRES, flexible GMRES, BiCGSTAB, MINRES and other methods appropriate to the matrix structure.
Convergence controls should include relative residual tolerance, absolute residual tolerance, maximum iteration count, stagnation detection, divergence detection and initial solution guess.

Preconditioning options should include Jacobi, block Jacobi, incomplete LU, incomplete Cholesky, algebraic multigrid, geometric multigrid, domain decomposition and suitable physics-based block preconditioners.
The solver should also support matrix conditioning diagnostics, scaling strategies, nullspace handling and detection of singular or nearly singular systems.

numGroups.title: Nonlinear solver parameters
numGroups.part: UNIVERSAL NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: The software should provide Newton–Raphson, damped Newton, quasi-Newton, Picard fixed-point iteration, nonlinear Krylov and trust-region methods where appropriate.

Typical numerical parameters should include maximum nonlinear iterations, absolute residual tolerance, relative residual tolerance, solution update tolerance, initial damping factor, line-search strategy, trust-region radius and convergence norm.

For difficult nonlinear problems, additional controls should include continuation parameters, load increment size, pseudo-transient continuation, arc-length continuation, tangent matrix update frequency and nonlinear stabilisation.
Contact, plasticity, fracture, chemical reaction, phase transition and nonlinear metamaterial switching can require specialised convergence parameters.
The software should permit separate convergence monitoring for temperature, concentration, pressure, displacement, electric potential and other coupled variables, with appropriate scaling.

numGroups.title: Multiphysics coupling and solver partitioning
numGroups.part: UNIVERSAL NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: Typical parameters should include the selected coupling strategy, monolithic or segregated solution, coupling iteration count, field update sequence, coupling relaxation and convergence thresholds.
For partitioned solvers, the software should support fixed relaxation, Aitken relaxation, under-relaxation, strong and weak coupling, staggered iterations and coupling acceleration.
Field transfer controls should include interpolation order, conservative mapping, projection method, interface matching tolerance and transfer frequency.
The platform should support coupled time stepping, subcycling, asynchronous exchange where physically and numerically justified, and independent time scales for different physics.
The coupled solver should report per-field residuals, interfacial conservation errors, coupling convergence and sensitivity to coupling strategy.

numGroups.title: Density Functional Theory and quantum electronic calculations
numGroups.part: QUANTUM, ATOMIC AND MOLECULAR NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: The software should support exchange–correlation functional selection, pseudopotential type, basis-set family, basis size, plane-wave energy cutoff, charge density cutoff, reciprocal-space sampling and Brillouin-zone integration.

Typical numerical settings include Monkhorst–Pack k-point mesh dimensions, k-point spacing, electronic smearing method, smearing width, electronic occupation settings, self-consistent-field energy tolerance, charge density convergence tolerance, maximum electronic iterations and density mixing parameters.
Atomic relaxation settings should include ionic optimisation method, maximum ionic steps, force convergence tolerance, stress convergence tolerance and cell relaxation controls.
For spin-polarised calculations, engineers should specify spin treatment, initial magnetic moments, spin–orbit coupling settings, magnetic symmetry and noncollinear magnetism options.

For advanced calculations, additional settings may include DFT+U parameters, hybrid functional settings, dispersion corrections, constrained DFT settings, excited-state calculation options and appropriate convergence controls.
Outputs should include the convergence history needed to establish whether electronic and structural results are numerically reliable.

numGroups.title: Molecular dynamics simulation
numGroups.part: QUANTUM, ATOMIC AND MOLECULAR NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: Typical parameters should include the interatomic potential or force-field model, force cutoff radius, neighbour-list cutoff, neighbour-list skin distance, neighbour-list update frequency and long-range interaction solver settings.

The engineer should be able to specify atom count, molecular topology, simulation cell dimensions, periodicity, time step, total simulation steps, initial atomic velocities and velocity-generation seed.
Thermostat settings should include the selected temperature control method, thermostat target temperature, coupling time constant and thermostat group definitions.
Barostat settings should include target pressure, pressure relaxation time, compressibility assumptions and allowed simulation cell deformation.

Other numerical controls should include constraint solver tolerances, bond constraint iteration limits, trajectory output frequency, equilibration duration, production duration, sampling interval and energy conservation thresholds.
For rare-event processes, enhanced-sampling parameters, bias potentials, collective variables and transition-path sampling controls may be required.

numGroups.title: Molecular Monte Carlo and kinetic Monte Carlo
numGroups.part: QUANTUM, ATOMIC AND MOLECULAR NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: Monte Carlo parameters should include total trial moves, equilibration steps, production steps, sampling interval, move proposal distributions, trial displacement magnitude, acceptance criteria and random seed.
For kinetic Monte Carlo, users should specify the event catalogue, event rates, reaction barriers, spatial lattice or site representation, event update strategy and simulation stopping conditions.

Additional settings may include temperature schedule, chemical potential reservoirs, particle insertion and deletion frequencies, adsorption site distributions, rejection thresholds and rare-event acceleration parameters.
For crystal growth and diffusion simulations, the event resolution must be sufficient to represent the selected migration, attachment, detachment, reaction and nucleation mechanisms.

numGroups.title: Quantum transport and advanced electronic calculations
numGroups.part: QUANTUM, ATOMIC AND MOLECULAR NUMERICAL SIMULATION PARAMETERS
text: The software should support electronic energy grid resolution, transport energy window, momentum-space discretisation, electrode or contact region definition, convergence tolerance for charge density, potential mixing and self-consistent transport iterations.

For nonequilibrium Green's function models, relevant parameters include lead self-energy convergence, energy integration accuracy, broadening parameters, boundary contact models and treatment of scattering.
Advanced optical and excited-state calculations may require frequency grids, excited-state counts, broadening parameters, dielectric screening settings and spectral convergence thresholds.
Calculations involving electron–phonon coupling, phonon spectra or many-body corrections should provide their own convergence parameters and numerical sampling controls.

numGroups.title: Chemical reaction solver configuration
numGroups.part: CHEMICAL SYNTHESIS, NUCLEATION, PARTICLE EVOLUTION AND MICROSTRUCTURE SIMULATION
text: Typical parameters should include reaction-network size, number of species, reaction equation indexing, reaction-rate evaluation method, numerical stiffness handling, nonlinear reaction solver selection and local chemistry solver tolerances.

The software should allow specification of maximum reaction substeps, local absolute and relative species tolerances, chemical equilibrium solver tolerance, reaction integration scheme and allowable concentration floors.
For highly stiff reaction systems, implicit integration and adaptive reaction subcycling should be supported.

Other settings should include reaction Jacobian approximation method, numerical versus analytic Jacobian selection, Jacobian reuse frequency, equilibrium iteration count and chemically conservative projection where appropriate.
For reactive transport, the platform should support fully coupled reaction–transport integration, sequential non-iterative splitting, iterative splitting and operator-splitting error control.

numGroups.title: Nucleation and crystal growth numerical parameters
numGroups.part: CHEMICAL SYNTHESIS, NUCLEATION, PARTICLE EVOLUTION AND MICROSTRUCTURE SIMULATION
text: The software should allow selection of homogeneous or heterogeneous nucleation formulations, deterministic or stochastic nucleation, local nucleation resolution, critical size discretisation and nucleation event sampling.

Population-based models should support particle-size bin count, minimum particle size, maximum particle size, bin spacing, sectional discretisation, moment closure method and population balance solver method.

For crystal growth calculations, parameters should include interface discretisation, growth-front update interval, facet resolution, growth anisotropy resolution, moving-boundary update frequency and allowable interface displacement per time step.
Stochastic models should permit random number seeds, ensemble size, nucleation event limits and convergence criteria for ensemble statistics.
Morphology predictions should include numerical settings for particle coalescence, aggregation, fragmentation and conservation of solid material.

numGroups.title: Population balance and particle distribution simulation
numGroups.part: CHEMICAL SYNTHESIS, NUCLEATION, PARTICLE EVOLUTION AND MICROSTRUCTURE SIMULATION
text: Typical numerical settings should include number of particle-size classes, bin distribution type, class boundaries, maximum number of internal coordinates, interpolation method and quadrature order.
For moment methods, the software should allow selection of the number of tracked moments, quadrature nodes, closure algorithms and moment-realizability checks.
For sectional population balance methods, controls should include aggregation kernel integration accuracy, growth flux interpolation, breakage source discretisation and numerical diffusion limits.
For Monte Carlo particle population simulation, parameters should include representative particle count, resampling frequency, random seed and statistical convergence limits.
The software should monitor total particle number, particle mass and distribution moments where physically conserved.

numGroups.title: Phase-field and microstructure evolution
numGroups.part: CHEMICAL SYNTHESIS, NUCLEATION, PARTICLE EVOLUTION AND MICROSTRUCTURE SIMULATION
text: Typical parameters should include phase-field mesh spacing, interface thickness resolution, diffuse-interface width, gradient-energy numerical treatment and interface mobility discretisation.

The platform should support the number of order parameters, interpolation function selection, phase-field solver type, time integration order, stabilisation coefficients and free-energy minimisation tolerances.
For grain growth, users should be able to specify the number of initial grains, orientation discretisation, grain boundary tracking resolution and remeshing or regridding interval.

Additional controls should include anti-trapping correction settings where applicable, mass conservation tolerance, phase-field boundedness limits, elastic coupling frequency and numerical interface-width sensitivity analysis.

numGroups.title: Sintering, coarsening and phase transformation numerics
numGroups.part: CHEMICAL SYNTHESIS, NUCLEATION, PARTICLE EVOLUTION AND MICROSTRUCTURE SIMULATION
text: The software should support time-step refinement for rapid neck growth, particle coalescence, pore closure and phase transitions.

Typical parameters include interface tracking tolerance, grain-boundary curvature resolution, phase fraction convergence thresholds, phase transformation event detection, solidification-front update frequency and mass conservation thresholds.

For particle-resolved sintering, settings may include contact discretisation, particle pair interaction update frequency, topology-change frequency and transition between separate and connected solid regions.
The platform should support adaptive refinement at rapidly evolving grain boundaries, pores, cracks and phase interfaces.

numGroups.title: Computational Fluid Dynamics numerical parameters
numGroups.part: FLUID DYNAMICS, POROUS MEDIA AND THERMAL SIMULATION
text: Typical CFD parameters should include flow solver type, pressure-based or density-based formulation, compressible or incompressible treatment, pressure–velocity coupling algorithm and convection discretisation scheme.
The platform should support SIMPLE, SIMPLEC, PISO and coupled pressure–velocity methods where suitable.

Other controls include pressure interpolation scheme, velocity reconstruction scheme, momentum relaxation factors, pressure relaxation factors, density interpolation, turbulence discretisation, pressure correction tolerance and mass conservation criterion.
For transient CFD, the engineer should specify Courant number limits, maximum iterations per time step, temporal discretisation order and adaptive time-step settings.
For turbulent flows, settings should include turbulence closure model, wall treatment, near-wall mesh resolution, wall function selection and model-specific numerical tolerances.

For multiphase flow, parameters should include interface compression controls, volume fraction boundedness, phase coupling iteration count, surface tension discretisation and phase-interface refinement.

numGroups.title: Porous-media and pore-scale flow numerical parameters
numGroups.part: FLUID DYNAMICS, POROUS MEDIA AND THERMAL SIMULATION
text: The software should support Darcy-scale, Brinkman-scale, Forchheimer-scale and pore-resolved models.

Numerical settings should include permeability field interpolation, porosity discretisation, pore-network node count, throat count, pore-to-pore connectivity, pore geometry resolution and hydraulic solver tolerance.
For pore-resolved simulations, engineers should configure the minimum number of cells across relevant pore throats, wall boundary resolution and pore-scale pressure convergence.
For coupled pore pressure and deformation, additional parameters include pore-fluid/solid solver coupling tolerances, effective stress update frequency and mass balance error limits.
For evolving porous microstructures, the software should provide geometry update frequency, permeability recalculation interval, porosity update threshold and mesh adaptation controls.

numGroups.title: Lattice Boltzmann numerical parameters
numGroups.part: FLUID DYNAMICS, POROUS MEDIA AND THERMAL SIMULATION
text: Typical settings should include lattice topology, lattice resolution, collision operator, relaxation time, distribution function initialisation and streaming algorithm.
The platform should support common discrete velocity lattices, single-relaxation-time and multiple-relaxation-time collision models, and other stable collision formulations where implemented.

Further parameters include boundary interpolation order, lattice time step, lattice Mach number limits, viscosity mapping, forcing scheme, multiphase interaction parameter discretisation and fluid–solid boundary treatment.
For thermal or multispecies lattice Boltzmann simulations, additional relaxation parameters and separate distribution functions may be necessary.
The software should monitor numerical stability, compressibility error and conservation performance.

numGroups.title: Discrete Element Method and particle-resolved simulation
numGroups.part: FLUID DYNAMICS, POROUS MEDIA AND THERMAL SIMULATION
text: DEM numerical controls should include particle count, particle geometry representation, contact detection algorithm, contact neighbour-list update frequency and particle time step.
Other parameters should include contact integration method, collision resolution, overlap tolerance, contact stiffness treatment, numerical damping and frictional contact convergence.

For coupled CFD–DEM calculations, the software should support fluid–particle coupling time intervals, interpolation methods, particle force averaging, momentum conservation tolerances and mesh-to-particle resolution controls.
For cohesive nanoparticle systems, additional numerical handling may be required for van der Waals interactions, electrostatic forces, particle adhesion, Brownian motion and agglomeration.

numGroups.title: Heat transfer numerical parameters
numGroups.part: FLUID DYNAMICS, POROUS MEDIA AND THERMAL SIMULATION
text: Typical settings should include conduction solver type, energy equation discretisation order, transient thermal integration, thermal nonlinear iteration limits and temperature convergence tolerances.

For conjugate heat transfer, the software should support separate solid and fluid thermal meshes, interface temperature and heat-flux transfer methods, coupling iterations and under-relaxation factors.
For radiation, parameters should include angular discretisation, spectral discretisation, number of rays or directions, radiation iteration limits and radiative transfer convergence criteria.

For laser, microwave or plasma heating, the numerical controls should include power-source spatial resolution, time-dependent excitation resolution, coupled electromagnetic–thermal update frequency and source interpolation.
For nanoscale phonon transport, angular and frequency sampling, phonon-mode resolution and scattering solver tolerances should be configurable.
For phase change, the platform should support interface tracking, latent heat treatment, phase fraction convergence and moving-boundary resolution.

numGroups.title: Electrostatic and electric-current solver parameters
numGroups.part: ELECTRICAL, ELECTROMAGNETIC, OPTICAL AND MAGNETIC SIMULATION
text: The software should allow direct or iterative solution of the electric potential field, numerical discretisation order, charge conservation tolerance and electrical current balance threshold.
Parameters should include conductivity matrix assembly, nonlinear conductivity iteration, electric-field interpolation order and field gradient recovery.
For electrochemical and semiconductor problems, separate numerical tolerances should be available for potential, carrier concentrations, ionic species and electrode reaction currents.
For electrical breakdown or strongly field-dependent behaviour, adaptive refinement should be provided around high-field regions and material interfaces.

numGroups.title: Semiconductor drift–diffusion and quantum electronic transport
numGroups.part: ELECTRICAL, ELECTROMAGNETIC, OPTICAL AND MAGNETIC SIMULATION
text: Typical settings should include carrier transport discretisation, electron and hole continuity solver tolerances, mobility model update frequency, recombination solver controls and Poisson–carrier coupling iterations.
The software should support Scharfetter–Gummel discretisation and other appropriate stabilised semiconductor transport methods.
For quantum-corrected semiconductor models, relevant settings include quantum correction discretisation, self-consistent iteration limits, energy-state resolution and interface treatment.
Transient electronic simulations should resolve carrier lifetimes, charging events and device switching dynamics through appropriate time-step controls.

numGroups.title: Frequency-domain electromagnetic simulation
numGroups.part: ELECTRICAL, ELECTROMAGNETIC, OPTICAL AND MAGNETIC SIMULATION
text: Typical parameters should include frequency range, number of frequency samples, linear or logarithmic frequency spacing, adaptive frequency sweep settings and resonance search tolerances.

The solver should support electromagnetic polynomial order, curl-conforming finite elements, complex-valued material properties, frequency-dependent interpolation and solver settings for indefinite linear systems.
For metamaterial unit cells, controls should include periodic boundary mapping, Bloch phase evaluation, scan-angle sampling, polarisation selection and reciprocal-space path discretisation.
For resonant modes, the software should allow target eigenfrequency, eigenmode count, eigensolver tolerance, spectral shift and resonance quality-factor extraction settings.
For absorbing layers, it should include perfectly matched layer thickness, stretching profile, polynomial order and reflection convergence controls.

numGroups.title: Time-domain electromagnetic simulation
numGroups.part: ELECTRICAL, ELECTROMAGNETIC, OPTICAL AND MAGNETIC SIMULATION
text: Typical parameters should include spatial grid resolution, time step, maximum Courant number, total simulated time, source waveform, source bandwidth and waveform sampling.

For finite-difference time-domain methods, the engineer should configure grid type, numerical dispersion limits, conformal boundary treatment, absorbing boundary thickness and electromagnetic material dispersion fitting.
The simulation should provide controls for monitoring electromagnetic field probes, energy flux surfaces, time-domain convergence, decay thresholds and Fourier transform windows.
For nonlinear and tunable electromagnetic materials, material state update frequency, coupled thermal or electrical time stepping and switching event resolution should also be provided.

numGroups.title: Optical and photonic simulation
numGroups.part: ELECTRICAL, ELECTROMAGNETIC, OPTICAL AND MAGNETIC SIMULATION
text: Typical parameters should include wavelength range, spectral resolution, optical mode count, diffraction order count, angular resolution, polarisation sampling and optical source bandwidth.
For rigorous coupled-wave analysis, engineers should control Fourier harmonic count, layer discretisation, convergence tolerance and scattering matrix stability.
For photonic crystal band calculations, the software should permit Brillouin-zone path definition, wave-vector sampling, number of eigenmodes and mode convergence thresholds.
For plasmonic simulations, local refinement should resolve narrow gaps, metallic surfaces, high field gradients and nanoscale interfaces.
Where nonlocal, hydrodynamic or quantum corrections are used, the additional numerical variables and boundary requirements must be handled by the relevant specialised solver.

numGroups.title: Micromagnetic and magnetic material simulation
numGroups.part: ELECTRICAL, ELECTROMAGNETIC, OPTICAL AND MAGNETIC SIMULATION
text: The software should allow the number of magnetic cells, magnetic mesh size, exchange length resolution, spin integration time step and magnetisation convergence tolerance to be specified.
Other parameters should include demagnetisation field solver method, magnetic energy minimisation tolerance, damping treatment, stochastic thermal field sampling and magnetic-field sweep resolution.
For magnetic hysteresis calculations, the engineer should specify field increment size, number of sweep points, equilibrium tolerance at each field and switching event detection parameters.
For spin transport, numerical settings should include spin diffusion discretisation, coupling to charge transport and interface transfer accuracy.

numGroups.title: Structural finite-element solver parameters
numGroups.part: STRUCTURAL, ACOUSTIC AND METAMATERIAL SIMULATION
text: Typical controls should include displacement interpolation order, stress recovery method, nonlinear geometry activation, constitutive integration algorithm and equilibrium iteration limits.
For plasticity, parameters should include return-mapping algorithm, material integration tolerance, plastic correction iteration limit and consistent tangent calculation.
For large deformation, engineers should specify updated or total Lagrangian formulation, element distortion monitoring, contact search strategy and load-step adaptation.

For shell and beam metamaterial lattices, settings should include beam theory selection, cross-section integration, rotational degrees of freedom, shell thickness integration and shear-locking controls.
For nearly incompressible materials, appropriate mixed formulations, stabilisation and volumetric locking controls should be provided.

numGroups.title: Contact, fracture and damage simulation
numGroups.part: STRUCTURAL, ACOUSTIC AND METAMATERIAL SIMULATION
text: The software should support contact detection tolerances, contact search frequency, penetration tolerances, penalty factors, augmented Lagrangian parameters and friction regularisation.
For cohesive-zone models, numerical parameters should include interface element resolution, damage regularisation, separation update tolerance and softening integration.
For phase-field fracture, engineers should specify crack regularisation length, mesh resolution relative to that length, fracture solver coupling scheme and irreversibility enforcement settings.
For extended finite-element or crack tracking methods, settings should include enrichment functions, crack growth increments, crack-front tracking and remeshing tolerances.
Damage analyses should monitor energy balance, convergence under softening, mesh dependence and physically appropriate damage evolution.

numGroups.title: Modal, harmonic and transient structural dynamics
numGroups.part: STRUCTURAL, ACOUSTIC AND METAMATERIAL SIMULATION
text: Typical parameters should include number of requested eigenmodes, eigenfrequency search interval, eigenvalue solver method, eigensolver tolerance and modal normalisation.
For harmonic response, settings should include frequency range, frequency step size, damping representation and resonance refinement.
For transient dynamics, parameters should include integration method, time step, mass matrix treatment, numerical damping and stability constraints.
For impact and explicit structural simulations, stable time increment, mass scaling, contact update frequency, hourglass control and artificial energy monitoring should be configurable.
For mechanical metamaterials, the solver should handle unstable or nearly unstable modes, bifurcation detection and continuation through snap-through transitions.

numGroups.title: Acoustic and phononic numerical parameters
numGroups.part: STRUCTURAL, ACOUSTIC AND METAMATERIAL SIMULATION
text: The software should provide acoustic mesh resolution relative to the minimum wavelength, polynomial interpolation order, frequency sweep controls and complex acoustic material parameters.
For acoustic eigenvalue and phononic band calculations, settings should include reciprocal-space path, Bloch wave-vector sampling, eigenmode count, modal convergence and band tracking.
For viscothermal acoustic models, engineers should specify boundary-layer mesh resolution, frequency-domain or time-domain formulation and numerical tolerances.
For acoustic–structure interaction, coupling iteration controls, interface transfer accuracy and damping consistency should be supported.
For finite acoustic metamaterial structures, perfectly matched layers, radiation boundary placement and outgoing wave accuracy must be checked.

numGroups.title: Metamaterial effective property retrieval and homogenisation
numGroups.part: STRUCTURAL, ACOUSTIC AND METAMATERIAL SIMULATION
text: Typical parameters should include unit-cell size, representative volume dimensions, periodicity, unit-cell mesh resolution, selected loading cases and homogenisation method.
For mechanical homogenisation, the numerical configuration should specify independent macroscopic strain or stress states, boundary condition type and averaging method.
For electromagnetic metamaterials, the software should permit frequency sampling, scattering parameter retrieval method, branch selection strategy and effective-medium validity checks.
For acoustic and elastic metamaterials, controls should include wave-vector discretisation, mode selection, spatial dispersion treatment and frequency-dependent effective-property fitting.
Outputs should be checked for passivity, causality where relevant, symmetry, energy consistency, numerical convergence and appropriate scale separation.

numGroups.title: Finite metamaterial arrays and large architectures
numGroups.part: STRUCTURAL, ACOUSTIC AND METAMATERIAL SIMULATION
text: The software should support explicit unit-cell replication, supercell modelling, representative periodic subdomains and homogenised continuum approximation.
Typical numerical parameters include the number of cells in each direction, supercell size, finite-array discretisation, edge refinement, interface coupling and domain decomposition settings.
For very large lattices, beam or shell idealisations, reduced-order modelling, substructuring and effective constitutive laws should be available.
For optical and electromagnetic arrays, the software should support finite aperture size, radiation domain extent, periodic approximation controls and array interaction resolution.
For acoustic and mechanical arrays, global modes, local resonances and boundary-induced wave reflections must be adequately resolved.

numGroups.title: Multiscale simulation numerical parameters
numGroups.part: MULTISCALE, COUPLED, LARGE-SCALE AND HIGH-PERFORMANCE COMPUTING
text: Typical parameters should include the number of model scales, coupling strategy, coarse-scale mesh size, fine-scale model size and representative volume dimensions.
The engineer should specify atomistic-to-continuum transfer frequency, homogenisation update interval, scale-bridging interpolation method and consistency constraints.
For concurrent coupling, settings should include overlap region thickness, handshake-region weighting, interface mapping tolerance and subcycling ratios.
For sequential coupling, the platform should define the property extraction method, interpolation of state-dependent properties and numerical error transfer between scales.
Convergence assessments should include both fine-scale and coarse-scale numerical accuracy.

numGroups.title: Reduced-order modelling and surrogate simulation
numGroups.part: MULTISCALE, COUPLED, LARGE-SCALE AND HIGH-PERFORMANCE COMPUTING
text: Numerical controls should include the number of retained reduced basis vectors, snapshot count, snapshot sampling strategy, projection method and approximation tolerance.
For proper orthogonal decomposition, reduced basis truncation criteria and captured variance targets should be configurable.
For reduced-basis and operator-inference approaches, numerical settings should include training domain, state dimension, parameter discretisation and regularisation strength.
Surrogate models should have defined training, validation and test datasets, input normalisation, extrapolation detection, prediction uncertainty and error thresholds.
Reduced-order results should be compared against high-fidelity simulations at representative operating conditions.

numGroups.title: High-performance computing and parallel processing
numGroups.part: MULTISCALE, COUPLED, LARGE-SCALE AND HIGH-PERFORMANCE COMPUTING
text: Typical parameters should include number of CPU cores, number of computing nodes, memory allocation, GPU selection, GPU memory limits and MPI process count.
Parallel numerical settings should include domain partitioning, load balancing, communication scheduling, distributed sparse matrix assembly and solver threading.
Additional controls should include checkpoint interval, checkpoint compression, restart capability, job wall-time limits, maximum memory usage, data output frequency and solver failure recovery.
For large atomistic or molecular simulations, parameters should include spatial decomposition, neighbour-list load balancing and accelerator configuration.
For large FEM and CFD cases, the platform should support partition-aware mesh distribution, scalable preconditioners and parallel file output.

numGroups.title: Numerical precision, reproducibility and execution determinism
numGroups.part: MULTISCALE, COUPLED, LARGE-SCALE AND HIGH-PERFORMANCE COMPUTING
text: The software should support single, double and, where necessary, higher numerical precision, together with mixed-precision computing.
Typical settings include floating-point tolerance, matrix scaling, deterministic reduction options, pseudo-random number seeds, numerical reproducibility level and hardware configuration logging.
The simulation records should preserve solver version, numerical library versions, algorithm settings, mesh identifiers, material model revisions and machine configuration.
For stochastic nucleation, particle dynamics, uncertainty analysis and AI-related calculations, random seeds and ensemble definitions should be recorded explicitly.

numGroups.title: Active tuning and control simulation parameters
numGroups.part: TUNING, CONTROL, FABRICATION AND INDUSTRIAL PROCESSES
text: The software should support controller sampling interval, control horizon, prediction horizon, control update frequency and actuator command limits.
For PID control, numerical parameters should include proportional, integral and derivative gain settings, derivative filtering, anti-windup configuration and command saturation.

For model predictive control, parameters should include optimisation horizon, state estimation frequency, control cost weights, physical constraints, solver tolerance and permitted control iterations.
For adaptive or robust control, engineers should specify parameter adaptation rates, estimator covariance, disturbance model, uncertainty bounds and stability constraints.
For programmable metamaterials, the system should support discrete state counts, switching thresholds, switching delays, hysteresis treatment and actuator coupling frequency.
Coupled control–physics simulations must resolve both the controller sample period and the physical system's relevant time scales.

numGroups.title: Fabrication process numerical parameters
numGroups.part: TUNING, CONTROL, FABRICATION AND INDUSTRIAL PROCESSES
text: The software should provide process-specific solver configuration for hydrothermal synthesis, solvothermal reactions, chemical bath deposition, CVD, PVD, ALD, electrodeposition, electrospinning, lithography, etching, sintering and additive manufacturing.

For hydrothermal and chemical bath reactors, numerical parameters should include species transport resolution, reaction integration tolerances, thermal time step, nucleation population resolution and growth-front tracking.
For CVD and plasma-enhanced processes, settings should include gas-phase reaction solver tolerances, surface reaction resolution, plasma transport discretisation and deposition front updates.
For sputtering and PVD, the platform may require particle trajectory sampling, angular distribution discretisation, deposition flux integration and surface geometry update frequency.
For lithography, numerical controls should include optical discretisation, exposure grid spacing, resist reaction solver tolerance, developer transport resolution and profile evolution accuracy.

For additive manufacturing, settings should include build layer discretisation, laser scan temporal resolution, moving heat-source integration, melt-pool mesh refinement, solidification time stepping and residual-stress calculation tolerances.

numGroups.title: Manufacturing process optimisation
numGroups.part: TUNING, CONTROL, FABRICATION AND INDUSTRIAL PROCESSES
text: Typical parameters should include process design variables, lower and upper parameter bounds, objective function weights, inequality and equality constraints, optimisation algorithm and stopping criteria.
Process objectives may include particle-size uniformity, nanorod alignment, deposition thickness, yield, energy use, manufacturing time, cost and defect minimisation.
The platform should support response surface methodology, gradient-based optimisation, Bayesian optimisation, genetic algorithms and surrogate-assisted optimisation.
Numerical controls should include optimisation population size, iteration count, candidate evaluation budget, constraint violation tolerance and convergence threshold.

numGroups.title: Industrial process control and digital twin parameters
numGroups.part: TUNING, CONTROL, FABRICATION AND INDUSTRIAL PROCESSES
text: The software should allow acquisition interval, process sensor update rate, filtering windows, model update frequency and data assimilation intervals to be configured.
Typical settings include state estimator tolerance, model calibration frequency, anomaly detection thresholds and predictive maintenance forecast horizon.

For digital twins, the engineer should specify the simulation latency budget, real-time numerical approximation method, reduced-order model update frequency and permissible divergence between measured and simulated states.
For manufacturing optimisation, plant-wide computation may require multiple operating scenarios, batch scheduling resolution, production capacity constraints and equipment availability modelling.

numGroups.title: Gradient-based optimisation parameters
numGroups.part: INVERSE DESIGN, REVERSE ENGINEERING AND OPTIMISATION
text: Typical numerical settings should include optimisation variables, design variable bounds, objective function scaling, constraint tolerance, gradient computation method and convergence tolerance.
The software should support analytic gradients, automatic differentiation, numerical finite-difference gradients and adjoint sensitivities where applicable.
Additional parameters should include line-search strategy, step size, trust-region radius, maximum iterations, regularisation coefficients and gradient norm stopping criteria.
For topology optimisation, design density filtering, minimum feature-size constraints, projection continuation and connectivity controls should be provided.

numGroups.title: Evolutionary and population-based optimisation
numGroups.part: INVERSE DESIGN, REVERSE ENGINEERING AND OPTIMISATION
text: The platform should support population size, number of generations, mutation rate, crossover probability, tournament or selection strategy, elitism count and random seed.
For particle swarm optimisation, settings should include swarm size, inertia weight, cognitive and social coefficients, velocity bounds and convergence criteria.
For differential evolution, relevant parameters include population size, mutation factor, crossover rate and candidate selection scheme.
Multiobjective optimisation should include Pareto archive size, crowding-distance handling, nondominated sorting, diversity preservation and hypervolume convergence thresholds.

numGroups.title: Bayesian optimisation and active learning
numGroups.part: INVERSE DESIGN, REVERSE ENGINEERING AND OPTIMISATION
text: Typical parameters should include surrogate model family, kernel type, kernel hyperparameters, training sample count, acquisition function, exploration–exploitation balance and optimisation budget.
The software should support expected improvement, probability of improvement, upper confidence bound and constrained acquisition functions where appropriate.
Additional controls should include observation noise, uncertainty calibration, candidate batch size, retraining frequency and stopping criteria.
For materials discovery, active learning should identify candidates where new experiments or high-fidelity simulations are expected to reduce uncertainty or improve material performance.

numGroups.title: Machine learning and physics-informed modelling
numGroups.part: INVERSE DESIGN, REVERSE ENGINEERING AND OPTIMISATION
text: The software should allow training dataset size, training–validation–test splitting, batch size, learning rate, training epochs, optimiser type, network depth, layer width and activation function to be configured.

For physics-informed neural networks, engineers should specify collocation point count, boundary-condition samples, initial-condition samples, physics loss weights, measurement loss weights, adaptive sampling criteria and optimisation strategy.
For graph neural networks, controls should include graph depth, message-passing layers, neighbourhood cutoff, node features and edge features.
For neural operators, parameters should include spatial resolution, Fourier modes or operator basis size, latent dimensions, training sequence length and generalisation testing.
The software must monitor overfitting, training instability, extrapolation and consistency with physical conservation requirements.

numGroups.title: Inverse parameter estimation and reverse engineering
numGroups.part: INVERSE DESIGN, REVERSE ENGINEERING AND OPTIMISATION
text: Typical parameters should include the set of unknown material parameters, initial estimates, admissible parameter bounds, observation data, measurement uncertainty and inverse model selection.
The software should support least-squares inversion, regularised inversion, Bayesian inference, adjoint inversion, derivative-free optimisation and simulation-based inference.
Numerical controls should include regularisation type, regularisation strength, maximum inverse iterations, stopping tolerance, parameter scaling and identifiability thresholds.

For geometry reconstruction, the software should support image segmentation resolution, voxel size, tomography projection count, reconstruction iteration count, denoising strength and geometric regularisation.

For metamaterial reverse engineering, numerical settings should include unit-cell search resolution, symmetry candidates, periodicity estimation tolerance, effective-property matching criteria and frequency-domain response fitting.
For reconstructing fabrication processes, the software should allow parameter ensembles, plausible process bounds, multiple candidate histories and uncertainty-weighted ranking.

numGroups.title: Stochastic and probabilistic numerical parameters
numGroups.part: STOCHASTIC SIMULATION, UNCERTAINTY AND VALIDATION
text: The software should allow probability distribution selection, distribution parameters, random seed, stochastic field correlation length and spatial random field resolution.
For Monte Carlo analysis, settings should include sample count, convergence tolerance, confidence interval target and variance reduction method.
For Latin hypercube sampling, the platform should support sample size, stratification strategy and correlation handling.
For polynomial chaos expansion, parameters should include polynomial order, quadrature rule, sparse-grid level and truncation strategy.
For random material microstructures, engineers should specify ensemble size, statistical representativeness and convergence of effective properties across realisations.

numGroups.title: Sensitivity and uncertainty quantification
numGroups.part: STOCHASTIC SIMULATION, UNCERTAINTY AND VALIDATION
text: Typical settings should include local or global sensitivity method, selected uncertain variables, sample count, perturbation magnitude, sensitivity convergence tolerance and response quantities of interest.
For Sobol sensitivity indices, controls should include sampling strategy, estimator selection, confidence estimation and bootstrap sample count.
For uncertainty propagation, the software should permit correlated parameters, model-form uncertainty, numerical uncertainty and measurement uncertainty to be represented separately.
Outputs should include uncertainty intervals, sensitivity rankings and decomposition of uncertainty contributions.

numGroups.title: Numerical verification and convergence testing
numGroups.part: STOCHASTIC SIMULATION, UNCERTAINTY AND VALIDATION
text: The software should support automated mesh-convergence studies, time-step convergence studies, nonlinear solver tolerance studies and numerical order-of-accuracy assessment.
Typical controls include number of refinement levels, refinement ratio, selected output quantities, observed convergence thresholds and acceptable numerical error.
For manufactured solution tests, engineers should be able to specify the manufactured fields, analytical derivatives or symbolic evaluation settings, numerical norm and expected convergence order.
For conservation-law verification, the platform should monitor global and local conservation residuals and numerical source-term consistency.

numGroups.title: Experimental model calibration and validation
numGroups.part: STOCHASTIC SIMULATION, UNCERTAINTY AND VALIDATION
text: Typical parameters should include calibration dataset selection, independent validation dataset selection, measured input uncertainty, observed output uncertainty, fitting method and residual weighting.
The software should provide controls for parameter bounds, optimisation iterations, likelihood model, error covariance and calibration stopping criteria.
Validation metrics should include RMSE, MAE, relative error, normalised error, correlation measures, bias and other application-appropriate statistical comparisons.
For metamaterials, validation sampling should cover relevant excitation frequency, incidence angle, amplitude, temperature and manufacturing variability.
For nanomaterial synthesis, validation should cover measured growth rate, particle-size distribution, crystal phase, morphology, reaction conversion and relevant physical properties.

numGroups.title: Numerical solver outputs
numGroups.part: OUTPUT DATA FROM NUMERICAL SIMULATION SETTINGS
text: Typical outputs should include total degrees of freedom, node and element counts, mesh quality statistics, number of linear iterations, nonlinear iteration histories, residual norms, convergence status, solver warnings and numerical failure reasons.

The platform should record the actual time-step history, accepted and rejected time steps, minimum and maximum time steps, nonlinear damping adjustments, continuation steps and numerical stability monitoring.
For multiphysics calculations, separate residuals and coupling errors should be reported for each dependent field.

numGroups.title: Numerical accuracy and verification outputs
numGroups.part: OUTPUT DATA FROM NUMERICAL SIMULATION SETTINGS
text: The platform should generate grid-convergence plots, time-step convergence results, estimated discretisation errors, observed numerical accuracy, conservation errors, stability diagnostics and sensitivity to solver tolerance.
For frequency-domain and modal simulations, it should report frequency convergence, eigenmode convergence, modal residuals, resonance tracking and periodic-boundary consistency.
For atomistic and quantum calculations, it should report energy convergence, force convergence, pressure or stress convergence, electronic self-consistency and simulation sampling quality.

numGroups.title: Computational efficiency outputs
numGroups.part: OUTPUT DATA FROM NUMERICAL SIMULATION SETTINGS
