text: The software should provide total wall-clock runtime, CPU time, GPU execution time, memory consumption, peak memory, parallel efficiency, hardware utilisation, communication overhead, linear solver time, assembly time, file I/O time and checkpoint information.
It should also estimate computational cost for mesh refinement, larger models, longer time horizons and additional parameter sweeps.

numGroups.title: Reproducibility and audit outputs
numGroups.part: OUTPUT DATA FROM NUMERICAL SIMULATION SETTINGS
text: Each simulation should save the complete numerical configuration, material model versions, geometry and mesh identifiers, random seeds, solver version, hardware details, calculation timestamps and execution logs.
The resulting files should permit an engineer to reconstruct the model, repeat the calculation, inspect numerical assumptions and compare future revisions.

numModes.text: The application selects a compatible solver, initial mesh, discretisation and numerical tolerances using model-specific rules, while reporting its assumptions
The engineer selects the physics and principal numerical parameters, with automated checks and recommended settings
The user can configure detailed solver algorithms, convergence, coupling, numerical stabilisation, mesh strategies, model formulations and specialised computational settings

cvvGroups.title: Experimental data preparation and calibration datasets
text: The software should support the acquisition, storage, preprocessing and qualification of experimental data from SEM, TEM, STEM, AFM, XRD, XPS, Raman spectroscopy, FTIR, nanoindentation, mechanical testing, thermal measurements, electrical testing, optical spectroscopy, electrochemical testing, magnetic testing, acoustic measurements, manufacturing instrumentation and industrial process systems.

Calibration datasets should retain specimen identity, material composition, manufacturing history, experimental geometry, temperature, pressure, loading conditions, applied fields, instrument calibration records, measurement uncertainty, sampling frequency, test duration and laboratory provenance.

The software should provide measurement unit conversion, coordinate transformation, experimental time alignment, baseline correction, uncertainty-aware interpolation, noise characterisation, outlier investigation, replicate analysis and data quality screening.
Calibration, model-selection and validation datasets should be separated wherever possible, with explicit controls preventing accidental reuse of validation measurements during parameter fitting.

cvvGroups.title: Material-property calibration
text: The software should support estimation of density, elastic constants, thermal conductivity, heat capacity, electrical conductivity, dielectric properties, magnetic properties, optical dispersion, chemical diffusivity, surface energy, interfacial resistance, permeability, fracture parameters, damping and other material-specific properties.
Parameter fitting should accommodate temperature-dependent, frequency-dependent, pressure-dependent, strain-dependent, composition-dependent and time-dependent material behaviour.
It should support isotropic, orthotropic, anisotropic, heterogeneous, nonlinear, viscoelastic, elastoplastic, damage-dependent and metamaterial effective constitutive models.
Calibration should preserve physical constraints, material stability conditions and realistic parameter ranges.

cvvGroups.title: Chemical reaction and growth-model calibration
text: The software should calibrate chemical reaction-rate coefficients, activation energies, reaction orders, equilibrium parameters, adsorption rates, desorption rates, nucleation parameters, growth-rate coefficients, precursor depletion rates, surface attachment kinetics, diffusion-controlled growth and crystal facet evolution.
For particle populations, calibration should use measured particle-size distributions, particle concentrations, growth histories, aggregation rates, morphology and crystallographic properties.
For nanorod and nanowire synthesis, the software should fit growth predictions to measured length, diameter, aspect ratio, alignment, number density and formation time.
Models should be tested against different precursor concentrations, reaction times, temperatures, pressures and substrates to assess parameter transferability.

cvvGroups.title: Mechanical and structural constitutive calibration
text: The software should support calibration of elastic moduli, Poisson's ratios, anisotropic stiffness tensors, yield parameters, hardening laws, creep coefficients, viscoelastic relaxation times, fracture energies, interface strengths, cohesive-zone parameters, fatigue laws and damage evolution coefficients.

Suitable measurements include nanoindentation, microtensile tests, microcompression tests, bending tests, cyclic loading, creep, dynamic mechanical testing, resonant measurements and full-field displacement measurements.
For architected mechanical metamaterials, calibration should distinguish constituent material properties from architecture-dependent effective properties.
The software should also identify whether fitted parameters depend on specimen size, strain rate, manufacturing orientation or structural imperfections.

cvvGroups.title: Thermal and thermophysical calibration
text: The software should calibrate heat capacity, conductivity, diffusivity, thermal expansion, thermal contact resistance, surface emissivity, heat-transfer coefficients, latent heat, phase transition kinetics and nanoscale thermal transport parameters.

Calibration should use appropriate calorimetry, thermal diffusivity measurements, thermal conductivity measurements, thermal expansion tests, thermoreflectance measurements and controlled heating/cooling experiments.
For nanoscale systems, the software should assess whether conventional Fourier transport is adequate before calibrating more complex ballistic, phonon or nonlocal heat-transport models.

cvvGroups.title: Electrical, electrochemical and semiconductor calibration
text: Calibration should cover electrical conductivity, resistivity, carrier mobility, carrier concentration, recombination parameters, interface charge transfer, double-layer capacitance, exchange current density, electrochemical kinetic coefficients, ion mobility, dielectric relaxation and semiconductor contact behaviour.
The software should fit appropriate models to measured current–voltage curves, impedance spectra, Hall measurements, transient electrical responses, cyclic voltammetry and galvanostatic measurements.
Parameter estimates should account for electrode geometry, temperature, electrolyte composition, contact resistance and instrumentation uncertainty.

cvvGroups.title: Optical, electromagnetic and photonic calibration
text: The software should support calibration of wavelength-dependent refractive index, extinction coefficient, dielectric dispersion, effective permittivity, effective permeability, resonance frequency, damping, optical absorption, scattering, phase response and nonlinear optical coefficients.

Calibration measurements may include ellipsometry, UV–visible spectroscopy, photoluminescence, optical scattering, near-field measurements, electromagnetic S-parameters, microwave measurements and terahertz spectroscopy.

For electromagnetic metamaterials, parameter retrieval should account for finite sample thickness, periodicity, incidence angle, polarisation, spatial dispersion and potential ambiguity in effective parameters.

cvvGroups.title: Acoustic, phononic and vibration calibration
text: Calibration should include acoustic impedance, damping, sound speed, dynamic stiffness, resonator mass and spring parameters, absorption coefficients, transmission loss and frequency-dependent effective density or modulus.
The software should use measured frequency-response functions, acoustic transmission data, modal tests, laser vibrometry, shaker tests and mechanical resonance measurements.
Metamaterial resonators should be calibrated over the relevant frequency and amplitude ranges, including nonlinear or hysteretic response where observed.

cvvGroups.title: Fabrication and manufacturing calibration
text: The platform should calibrate deposition rates, etch rates, growth rates, sintering kinetics, curing shrinkage, laser processing parameters, thermal contact conditions, coating thickness evolution, manufacturing defect distributions and equipment-dependent process correlations.
Calibration should use actual reactor sensor data, production batch records, thickness measurements, microscopy, profilometry, chemical analysis and fabrication yield data.
Separate parameter sets may be necessary for different reactors, equipment designs, substrates, materials and manufacturing scales.

cvvGroups.title: Statistical, Bayesian and inverse calibration
text: The software should implement ordinary and weighted least-squares calibration, nonlinear regression, maximum likelihood estimation, Bayesian parameter inference, hierarchical Bayesian calibration, regularised inverse parameter estimation and robust fitting.

It should support parameter priors, physical parameter bounds, measurement covariance, correlated errors, parameter sensitivity, practical identifiability, parameter confidence intervals and posterior predictive checks.

Calibration reports should identify parameter correlations, nonunique parameter combinations, weakly informed parameters, extrapolation limits and experimental measurements needed to reduce uncertainty.

cvvGroups.title: Governing-equation and mathematical consistency verification
text: The software should verify that each implemented governing equation, constitutive model, source term, interface treatment and coupling law matches its documented mathematical formulation.

Verification activities should include dimensional consistency, unit checking, mathematical sign convention checks, coordinate-system consistency, tensor symmetry where applicable, correct variable definitions and valid constitutive coupling.
Models should be checked against applicable physical conservation laws, thermodynamic restrictions and mathematical well-posedness requirements.

cvvGroups.title: Code verification
text: Every numerical solver should undergo controlled test cases demonstrating correct implementation.

The verification suite should include analytical solutions, manufactured solutions, simplified model limits, benchmark boundary-value problems, known symmetry cases, exact conservation examples and suitably documented regression tests.
Test cases should cover individual physics modules before proceeding to fully coupled multiphysics systems.
The software should compare computed results with independently derived reference solutions and report pass/fail results using predefined numerical acceptance criteria.

cvvGroups.title: Spatial discretisation verification
text: The platform should implement mesh refinement and grid-independence testing for finite-element, finite-volume, finite-difference, spectral and other relevant methods.

Verification should examine solution changes with element size, mesh topology, interpolation order, local refinement, geometric curvature resolution, interface representation and numerical integration accuracy.

The system should estimate observed convergence rates, discretisation errors, solution sensitivity to mesh quality and whether the computed quantity of interest is sufficiently mesh independent for its intended use.
For nanoscale geometries, mesh refinement should specifically examine small gaps, interfaces, nanorod tips, defects, pores, thin films and high-gradient regions.

cvvGroups.title: Temporal discretisation verification
text: Transient simulations should undergo time-step refinement, integration-order verification and numerical stability checks.
The software should compare predictions obtained using progressively smaller time steps and different relevant time integration schemes.

Time-step convergence should be evaluated for temperature, concentration, pressure, stress, electromagnetic transients, crystal growth, nucleation, phase evolution, controller switching and other important quantities.
Stiff chemical and multiphysics systems should be tested for numerical stability, solver convergence and physically admissible transient behaviour.

cvvGroups.title: Linear and nonlinear solver verification
text: Verification should cover linear solver residual convergence, matrix conditioning, preconditioner effectiveness, nonlinear iteration accuracy, Jacobian consistency, Newton convergence and sensitivity to numerical tolerances.
The platform should check that a terminated calculation satisfies its required residual and solution-update criteria.
It should detect false convergence caused by inadequate equation scaling, excessively loose tolerance settings or solver stagnation.

cvvGroups.title: Conservation-law verification
text: The software should monitor conservation of mass, chemical elements, electric charge, momentum and energy wherever applicable.
For particle population models, the software should monitor conservation of material mass during aggregation, coalescence, growth and fragmentation.
For thermal simulations, it should compare accumulated energy, external energy transfer, internal heat sources and changes in stored thermal energy.
For atomistic systems, energy conservation should be checked under the appropriate dynamics and ensemble assumptions.
For coupled multiphysics, conservation must be assessed both within individual subdomains and across interfaces.

cvvGroups.title: Boundary-condition and initial-condition verification
text: The verification framework should test prescribed-value, prescribed-flux, mixed, periodic, Bloch–Floquet, symmetry, contact, moving-boundary, absorbing and coupled-interface conditions.
It should check that boundary assignments apply to the correct geometric entities, that periodic faces match correctly and that interface variables are transferred consistently.
Initial conditions should be examined for compatibility with the governing equations, constraints and imposed boundaries.
Electromagnetic and acoustic open boundaries should be tested for artificial reflections, while mechanical constraints should be examined for rigid-body modes and overconstraint.

cvvGroups.title: Multiphysics coupling verification
text: The software should separately verify each coupling interface, including electrothermal, thermomechanical, electrochemical–thermal, fluid–structure, chemical–thermal, crystal-growth–stress, electromagnetic–mechanical and acoustic–structural couplings.
Testing should include one-way and two-way coupling, monolithic and partitioned solution methods, staggered field updates and conservative transfer between different computational meshes.
Coupling verification should measure interface balance errors, transfer interpolation errors, sensitivity to coupling iteration count and convergence under increasing coupling strength.

cvvGroups.title: Geometry and mesh import verification
text: Geometry importers should be tested using reference CAD solids, atomic structures, crystal lattices, metamaterial unit cells, computational meshes, voxel volumes, lithography layouts and time-dependent geometries.

Verification should examine unit conversions, atomic coordinates, crystal periodicity, material region labels, node and element connectivity, surface normals, topology preservation, geometric tolerances and physical dimensions.
The software should identify corrupt files, inconsistent geometry, self-intersections, duplicate entities, open boundaries and invalid periodic lattice definitions.
Geometry conversion tests should quantify information lost during representation changes, particularly when converting atomic or voxel structures into continuum CAD and mesh representations.

cvvGroups.title: Numerical reproducibility and regression verification
text: The software should maintain automated regression tests for every solver and coupling implementation.
Tests should be repeated whenever the governing models, source code, numerical libraries, geometry translators or parallel computing architecture change.

The verification framework should support pinned software environments, archived reference results, tolerance-based numerical comparison, deterministic execution where feasible and reproducible random seeds.
Results obtained on different CPU, GPU and parallel configurations should be assessed against appropriate numerical tolerances rather than requiring universal bitwise identity.

cvvGroups.title: Quantum and atomistic benchmarks
text: The benchmark library should include crystalline solids with well-characterised lattice parameters, elastic constants, cohesive energies, phonon spectra and electronic properties.

Suitable benchmark classes include elemental metals, covalent semiconductors, ionic crystals, layered materials, selected oxide materials, simple molecular systems, surfaces, vacancies, grain boundaries and adsorbed molecules.

Numerical verification should cover basis-set convergence, electronic self-consistency, finite-size effects, k-point sampling, force calculations, statistical sampling and simulation time-step effects.
Validation should distinguish experimentally measured quantities from higher-level theoretical reference calculations.

cvvGroups.title: Chemical reaction and thermodynamic benchmarks
text: The library should contain analytically solvable simple reaction systems, equilibrium phase examples, reversible reactions, precipitation and dissolution cases, multicomponent chemical speciation problems and controlled reaction calorimetry datasets.
Validation should include measured concentration histories, temperature-dependent reaction rates, phase-equilibrium measurements, solubility and conversion data.
Tests should cover both reaction-limited and transport-limited regimes.

cvvGroups.title: Nucleation, growth and crystallisation benchmarks
text: The library should contain documented growth experiments for selected metal oxides, semiconductor nanocrystals, colloidal nanoparticles, nanowires and nanorods.
Validation data should include time-resolved particle-size distributions, crystal phase, growth rate, induction time, precursor depletion, number density and morphology.
Where available, the software should compare growth model predictions against independent in-situ and ex-situ observations.
The system should recognise that nucleation and growth parameters can be strongly material-, solvent-, substrate- and process-dependent.

cvvGroups.title: Fluid dynamics and porous-media benchmarks
text: Verification should use established laminar flow examples, channel flow, pressure-driven flow, diffusion, advection, flow through porous media and suitable coupled reaction–transport cases.
Validation should use measured pressure drops, flow velocities, residence times, particle transport and porous-medium permeability.
Where turbulent or multiphase conditions are relevant, the benchmark programme should include data matched to the intended closure models and flow regimes.

cvvGroups.title: Heat transfer benchmarks
text: The library should support one-dimensional and multidimensional conduction, transient cooling, composite conduction, conjugate heat transfer, radiation exchange, phase change and internal heat generation.
Validation should use measured temperature profiles, thermal diffusivities, conductivities, contact resistance and transient thermal responses.
Nanoscale benchmarks should include measurements suitable for phonon transport, thin-film conduction and interfacial thermal resistance where those models are used.

cvvGroups.title: Electrical and electrochemical benchmarks
text: Verification should include known electrostatic fields, conduction in simple geometries, diffusion–migration problems, semiconductor transport benchmarks and electrochemical reaction limits.
Validation should use measured current–voltage curves, electrochemical impedance, carrier transport, charge storage, electrode reaction rates and deposition measurements.

cvvGroups.title: Electromagnetic, optical and photonic benchmarks
text: Verification should use analytically characterised electromagnetic wave propagation, scattering from simple geometries, waveguide modes, dielectric interfaces, resonant cavities and periodic unit cells.
Optical and electromagnetic metamaterial validation should use measured reflection, transmission, absorption, resonance, phase, polarisation and angular response.
Effective-property retrieval should be checked against physically meaningful reference systems and assessed for spatial dispersion, finite-thickness effects, passivity and causality.

cvvGroups.title: Structural mechanics and fracture benchmarks
text: The library should include patch tests, classical beam and plate problems, elasticity solutions, contact benchmarks, nonlinear deformation, buckling, dynamic vibration and fracture.
Validation should use measured load–displacement data, nanoindentation, microcompression, tensile tests, buckling experiments, crack-growth tests and fatigue measurements.
Architected metamaterials should be evaluated using both idealised reference geometries and as-manufactured specimens containing realistic imperfections.

cvvGroups.title: Acoustic and phononic benchmarks
text: Verification should cover plane waves, acoustic cavities, layered media, elastic-wave propagation and Bloch dispersion for periodic structures.
Validation should use measured sound absorption, transmission loss, resonance frequencies, vibration attenuation and phononic bandgaps.
Testing should examine frequency dependence, damping, manufacturing tolerances, specimen supports and finite-size effects.

cvvGroups.title: Phase-field and microstructure benchmarks
text: Verification should include interface evolution, grain growth, phase separation, conserved transport, solidification and suitable analytical or manufactured solutions.
Validation should compare predicted grain sizes, phase fractions, interface positions and morphological evolution against time-resolved experiments.
The benchmark programme should also examine sensitivity to diffuse-interface thickness, mesh resolution and assumed interface mobility.

cvvGroups.title: Control, tuning and programmable material benchmarks
text: The software should test control stability and numerical implementation on simplified dynamic systems with known responses.
Physical validation should use actuated specimens and tunable metamaterial prototypes with measured switching behaviour.
Tests should cover response time, tuning range, hysteresis, controller tracking, energy consumption, thermal effects, actuator saturation and repeated switching.

cvvGroups.title: Fabrication and industrial-scale benchmarks
text: The validation library should include reproducible laboratory and pilot-scale fabrication cases covering hydrothermal growth, thin-film deposition, chemical vapour deposition, atomic layer deposition, electrochemical deposition, lithography, sintering and additive manufacturing where suitable data exist.
Measured data should include process conditions, output geometry, product purity, film thickness, particle-size distributions, yield, energy use and defect statistics.
Industrial scale-up validation should demonstrate agreement not only at laboratory conditions but also across the geometries and operating ranges relevant to production.

cvvGroups.title: Reverse-engineering benchmarks
text: The software should maintain reconstruction benchmarks involving known atomic structures, calibrated tomography phantoms, measured nanostructures, defective lattices, metasurface patterns and specimens with known manufacturing conditions.
Tests should include controlled image noise, incomplete measurements, limited-angle tomography, missing geometric features, uncertain materials and nonunique inverse problems.

Performance should be judged using structural reconstruction error, property prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, identifiability and the ability to reproduce independent experimental responses.

cvvGroups.title: Sources of uncertainty
cvvGroups.part: UNCERTAINTY QUANTIFICATION, SENSITIVITY AND PREDICTIVE CREDIBILITY
text: The software should identify and distinguish uncertainty arising from material composition, purity, defect concentration, geometry, manufacturing tolerances, laboratory measurements, kinetic parameters, constitutive models, boundary conditions, initial conditions, numerical discretisation, stochastic physical processes and extrapolation.
It should distinguish variability inherent in manufacturing from uncertainty caused by insufficient knowledge.

For example, variation in particle size between production batches is different from uncertainty in the measured mean particle size, and both are different from error in the mathematical growth model.

cvvGroups.title: Sensitivity analysis
cvvGroups.part: UNCERTAINTY QUANTIFICATION, SENSITIVITY AND PREDICTIVE CREDIBILITY
text: The platform should support local sensitivity analysis, one-factor-at-a-time analysis, finite-difference sensitivity, analytic or automatic differentiation, adjoint sensitivity, variance-based global sensitivity, Sobol indices, Morris screening and derivative-based global sensitivity.

Sensitivity studies should identify which parameters most strongly influence nanorod dimensions, reaction conversion, lattice stiffness, effective Poisson's ratio, thermal conductivity, resonance, bandgap, fabrication yield, service life and other outputs.
It should identify parameters whose effects are correlated or practically indistinguishable.

cvvGroups.title: Parameter identifiability
cvvGroups.part: UNCERTAINTY QUANTIFICATION, SENSITIVITY AND PREDICTIVE CREDIBILITY
text: The software should evaluate structural and practical identifiability of model parameters.

It should support parameter correlation analysis, sensitivity matrix rank analysis, profile likelihood, Fisher information analysis, Bayesian posterior analysis and experimental design recommendations.
When two parameters cannot be estimated independently from available measurements, the software should report that limitation and recommend additional observables or experiments.

cvvGroups.title: Uncertainty propagation
cvvGroups.part: UNCERTAINTY QUANTIFICATION, SENSITIVITY AND PREDICTIVE CREDIBILITY
text: The platform should implement Monte Carlo sampling, Latin hypercube sampling, polynomial chaos expansion, surrogate-based propagation, Bayesian predictive inference and other suitable probabilistic methods.
It should propagate input uncertainties through chemical, mechanical, thermal, electrical, electromagnetic, acoustic, manufacturing and multiscale calculations.

Outputs should include probability distributions, confidence or credible intervals as appropriate, prediction intervals, uncertainty envelopes, sensitivity rankings and probability-of-failure estimates.

cvvGroups.title: Experimental design for reducing uncertainty
cvvGroups.part: UNCERTAINTY QUANTIFICATION, SENSITIVITY AND PREDICTIVE CREDIBILITY
text: The software should recommend experiments that improve parameter identifiability and reduce predictive uncertainty.

Examples include additional reaction temperatures to separate kinetic parameters, different precursor concentrations to identify reaction orders, mechanical tests at several strain rates to calibrate viscoelastic behaviour, and metamaterial measurements at multiple frequencies and incidence angles to distinguish competing electromagnetic models.
The framework should support design of experiments, factorial designs, response surface experimental plans, optimal experimental design, sequential Bayesian experiment selection and active learning.

cvvGroups.title: Validation-domain and extrapolation assessment
cvvGroups.part: UNCERTAINTY QUANTIFICATION, SENSITIVITY AND PREDICTIVE CREDIBILITY
text: Every calibrated or validated model should have a documented range of materials, compositions, temperatures, pressures, frequencies, geometric dimensions, strain rates, manufacturing methods and operating conditions over which supporting evidence exists.
The software should flag predictions made outside these ranges.
Extrapolation should be clearly identified, and increased uncertainty alone should not be presented as sufficient evidence that the extrapolated model remains physically valid.

cvvGroups.title: Recommended validation metrics
text: The software should automatically calculate appropriate metrics for the selected outputs.

Acceptance criteria must be defined by the application, measurement capability, consequence of error and intended engineering use. A universal percentage threshold would be inappropriate across all of these different phenomena.

cvvGroups.title: Centralised CVVUQ engine
text: Suite 24 should act as the central calibration, verification, validation and uncertainty engine for all 29 engineering suites.

It should provide shared services for experimental data management, test-case execution, numerical convergence assessment, parameter estimation, uncertainty propagation, benchmark comparison, result scoring, audit trails and qualification reporting.

Each physical solver should expose its governing model identity, parameter definitions, input units, numerical controls, calculated observables, sensitivities where available, convergence diagnostics and validation applicability information.

cvvGroups.title: Benchmark database and reference-data management
text: The software should maintain a version-controlled benchmark repository containing numerical reference problems, analytical solutions, manufactured solutions, experimentally measured datasets and representative engineering case studies.
Each benchmark should identify the relevant suite, material, geometry, operating conditions, physical model, numerical method, expected outputs, uncertainty and acceptance criteria.
Datasets should be linked to their original publications, laboratory records or qualified sources. Benchmark data should not be fabricated to fill gaps.

cvvGroups.title: Automated calibration and model fitting
text: Users should be able to import experimental observations, select uncertain parameters, define physical parameter bounds, choose a calibration method and initiate parameter estimation.
The software should produce fitted parameter values, uncertainty estimates, model–experiment comparisons, parameter correlation matrices and warnings about nonidentifiable parameters.
Parameter fits should be reproducible using saved data selections, fitting settings, model versions and random seeds.

cvvGroups.title: Automated verification test suite
text: Every solver implementation should have an automated test collection covering geometry import, numerical method correctness, analytical or manufactured solution comparisons, mesh and time-step refinement, conservation, boundary conditions, nonlinear convergence and coupled-interface consistency.
These tests should be executable during software development, continuous integration, version releases and after significant solver changes.

cvvGroups.title: Independent validation workflow
text: The software should allow engineers to register validation datasets that are separate from those used for calibration.
The system should reproduce the experimental geometry, material state, loading, temperature, pressure, fields, measurement positions and other relevant test conditions.
Predicted results should be compared with measured quantities using suitable statistical metrics and measurement uncertainties.
Validation should be tied to specific model versions and parameter sets, so that subsequent changes do not silently inherit previous validation claims.

cvvGroups.title: Model credibility and qualification records
text: Each physical model should have a documented credibility record describing its governing equations, assumptions, parameter sources, verified numerical behaviour, experimental validation evidence, known limitations and applicable operating ranges.
The software should allow classification of results such as:
These labels should represent evidence-backed states, not marketing claims.

cvvGroups.title: Failure handling and credibility warnings
text: The platform should automatically warn when essential physical inputs are missing, material parameters fall outside their calibrated range, the geometry is invalid, conservation checks fail, solver convergence is inadequate, mesh independence is unproven, experimental observations are inconsistent or a requested quantity cannot be identified uniquely.

It should also warn when an AI surrogate is used outside its training domain, when a homogenised metamaterial model is applied beyond its scale-separation assumptions and when predicted properties violate relevant physical admissibility constraints.

cvvGroups.title: Standard engineering verification and validation reports
text: Every qualified analysis should produce a report covering the material identity, geometry, physical models, calibration inputs, numerical setup, convergence evidence, uncertainty, independent validation comparisons, error metrics, applicability limits and final credibility assessment.
Recommended report deliverables include PDF, DOCX and HTML documents, with supporting CSV, XLSX, HDF5, VTK and other relevant numerical datasets.

A calculation input file is not always a standalone geometry file. For example, a Quantum ESPRESSO input may contain geometry, material assignments, calculation settings and other information.

principles: The platform should distinguish material property prediction from material fabrication simulation. Predicting a material's elastic modulus, optical response or thermal conductivity is a different computational task from predicting the conditions under which that material grows or forms.

It should distinguish intrinsic constituent properties from the effective properties of a metamaterial architecture. For instance, the base material may have a positive Poisson's ratio while an engineered lattice made from that material exhibits a negative effective Poisson's ratio.

Large-scale engineering analysis should not simply enlarge an atomic or nanoscale model. It should use appropriate multiscale transfer methods, homogenised constitutive properties and verified continuum models.

Tunability should be modelled with a physically achievable control mechanism and account for energy demand, response time, loss, reversibility, hysteresis, actuator limitations and switching durability.

Simulated results should be clearly classified as theoretical, calibrated, verified, experimentally validated or qualified for a specific application. A converged numerical solution is not sufficient evidence of physical accuracy.
